title: Progressive State Representative Wins Florida Democratic Senate Primary, Faces Republican Incumbent Moody
dek: Angie Nixon, a state representative and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, won Florida's Democratic Senate primary on August 18, 2026, defeating well-funded former National Security Council aide Alex Vindman. Nixon will face Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in the general election for a seat that represents the final two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio's term.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Angie Nixon, a progressive state representative and Democratic Socialist, won Florida's Democratic Senate primary on August 18, 2026, defeating Alex Vindman and advancing to face Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in the general election.
bottom_line: Nixon advances to November facing Moody in a state that favored Trump decisively in recent elections. The general election will test whether progressive messaging and ground organization can overcome historical Republican advantage in Florida statewide races.
body: Angie Nixon, a progressive state representative and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, won Florida's Democratic Senate primary on August 18, 2026, defeating Alex Vindman, a retired lieutenant colonel and Iraq War veteran who had been viewed as a heavy favorite heading into the contest, according to NBC News.

Nixon's victory reshapes the calculus of the general election. Vindman had raised more than $16 million for his campaign, per NBC News reporting, while Nixon brought in less than $1 million. Vindman was recruited to run by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in an effort to expand the party's map in a midterm election cycle expected to favor Democrats.

In her victory speech Tuesday night, Nixon told supporters: "We showed the world what organized people can accomplish. And we showed the world what people of Florida are all about. Medicare for all. Universal child care. Real, affordable housing. Fully funded public education. And an end to senseless wars." She also addressed Vindman's supporters directly, saying there is a place for them in her campaign, adding: "The great thing about our movement is we are not trying to force everyone to agree with us and believe exactly the same thing."

Vindman acknowledged the outcome in a statement, saying Nixon "ran a strong campaign" and pledging "I will be standing by her side in the fight against Ashley Moody." The DSCC released a supportive statement following Nixon's victory. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and DSCC Chair Kristen Gillibrand said in a joint statement: "Angie Nixon has dedicated her career to fighting for Florida. A lifelong native of Jacksonville and a former union organizer, Angie's dedication to put working families first runs deep, and now, she's running to take that fight to the Senate."

Nixon will face Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in the general election for a seat representing the final two years of the term Secretary of State Marco Rubio won in 2022. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed Moody to the seat last year after Trump selected Rubio for his Cabinet. Moody easily fended off several challengers to win her Republican primary Tuesday. In her victory speech, Moody accused Nixon of wanting to "destroy this country and everything that it is built on," stating: "We are staring down crazy and the socialists today." The National Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee spokesman Nick Puglia said: "Florida will never elect a socialist to the US Senate and we look forward to Ashley Moody's victory in November."

Nixon regularly criticized Vindman during the primary for only recently having moved to Florida. She framed her campaign as an attempt to prove that insurgent progressive politics has a place in Florida politics, posting on social media as a closing message: "Florida: the choice is OURS. We will decide our future, not billionaire donors or the establishment politics of DC." Vindman had largely ignored Nixon during the primary, the two never meeting for a debate, and attempted instead to focus on Moody.

A notable fault line in the race involves foreign policy. Nixon is an advocate for cutting U.S. aid to Israel, a controversial position in a state with the country's third-largest Jewish population and in contrast to Vindman, according to NBC News reporting. Nixon introduced a resolution in the state House calling for a "de-escalation and ceasefire in the state of Israel and occupied Palestine." She said she would have supported a congressional resolution in July that would have stripped $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel. When asked about her stance on WMNF radio in Tampa on Friday, Nixon said: "I would have voted in support of that, because we cannot continue to send money to countries that are violating international law, that are violating human rights, that are actively destroying." She also stated: "Throughout my adult career, I have fought for the safety and the well-being and the humanity of all people. And me stating this does not make me antisemitic at all."

Vindman came to national prominence as an aide to the National Security Council who gave congressional testimony about a 2019 call between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during which Trump was pushing for an investigation into Joe Biden, then a Democratic candidate for president. Vindman's testimony helped launch Trump's first impeachment by the House, though Trump was ultimately acquitted by the Senate. Vindman was later fired from the NSC.
